pos: adv. (a generalizing particle, standing apart from its pronoun in the Authorized Version: what man soever, what thing soever — the 1611 way of saying “any… at all”)
etymology: A compound of so and ever. In 1611 English the particle could stand detached from its interrogative — what man soever rather than whatsoever man — and the Authorized translators kept the separated form where the Hebrew put a word between. It renders the Hebrew ish ish, “a man, a man,” a doubling that means any man whatever.
biblical_def: The separated soever is one of the surest marks of the Authorized Version's age, and it is not a mannerism — it is following the Hebrew. The idiom ish ish, literally “a man, a man,” is Hebrew for any man at all, and the translators reproduced its structure: “What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp” (Leviticus 17:3). The same construction covers the priesthood: “What man soever of the seed of Aaron is a leper, or hath a running issue; he shall not eat of the holy things, until he be clean” (Leviticus 22:4) — the holiness of the office gave no exemption from the law of cleanness. Hushai uses it of intelligence to be passed to David: “what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests” (2 Samuel 15:35). And Moses uses it to close the law against tampering: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). In each case the particle does one job — it removes every exception.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soever as a word chiefly used in composition with who, what, where and how, and notes that it may be separated from these by an intervening word.
webster_full: SOEVER, a word compounded of so and ever, and annexed to who, what, where, how, as, whosoever, whatsoever, wheresoever, howsoever.
It may be separated from the pronoun or adverb by the intervening word; as, what man soever; how great soever.
WHOSOEVER, pron. Any person whatever.
WHATSOEVER, pron. Whatever; any thing that; being of any nature, kind or sort.
EVER, adv. At any time; at any period or point of time.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 12:32
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Leviticus 17:3
What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp,
Leviticus 22:4

What man soever of the seed of Aaron is a leper, or hath a running issue; he shall not eat of the holy things, until he be clean. And whoso toucheth any thing that is unclean by the dead, or a man whose seed goeth from him;
2 Samuel 15:35

And hast thou not there with thee Zadok and Abiathar the priests? therefore it shall be, that what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
corruption_summary: The Authorized Version's archaisms are treated as obstacles to be smoothed away, when several of them — this one included — are the translators reproducing the shape of the original.
corruption_paragraphs: It is often assumed that the Authorized Version's odd constructions are seventeenth-century English being quaint, and that a modern rendering loses nothing by regularising them. What man soever is a case where the assumption fails. The Hebrew ish ish is a doubling for emphasis, and the separated particle is the translators' attempt to let an English reader see that something is being doubled. Their preface, The Translators to the Reader, explains the policy at length: they aimed at a version transparent to the original, not at an elegant English composition, and they were willing to write awkward English to do it. The italics marking supplied words come from the same conviction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the particle is doing theologically, which is the removal of exceptions. Leviticus 22:4 is the sharpest instance: what man soever of the seed of Aaron — priestly descent conferred privilege and conferred no immunity, and a leprous priest ate no holy thing until he was clean. Deuteronomy 12:32 does the same for the law as a whole: not most things, not the important things, but what thing soever I command you. The old word is doing the work that the phrase without exception does now, and it is worth pausing over rather than translating past.
roots_summary: Hebrew ish ish, “a man, a man” — the doubling behind what man soever, Leviticus 17:3, 22:4; kol ha-dabar, the whole word or thing — Deuteronomy 12:32.
roots_lines: Hebrew ish ish — literally “a man, a man”; the emphatic doubling meaning any man whatever.
Hebrew kol — all, every, the whole; the generalizing word behind many of these constructions.
Hebrew dabar — a word or thing; Deuteronomy 12:32, “what thing soever.”
Greek hosos — as much as, whatsoever; the New Testament equivalent construction.
English so + ever; in 1611 the particle could stand apart from its pronoun.
usage: “What man soever” — the Hebrew doubling ish ish, reproduced in English.
“What man soever of the seed of Aaron” — priestly descent bought no exemption.
“What thing soever I command you” — the particle exists to remove exceptions.

pos: adv. (into which; an archaic relative of the Authorized Version, used of the land Caleb entered and of the boat the disciples took)
etymology: A compound of where and into, on the old English pattern that produced wherein, whereof, whereby, whereunto — a relative adverb standing for into which. The pattern is Germanic and was still ordinary written English in 1611.
biblical_def: The word is a plain relative — into which — and its most important occurrence rewards the reader who slows down for it. Of Caleb, after ten spies had brought back an evil report and the congregation had wept all night: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it” (Numbers 14:24). The precision is the point. Caleb had walked over that ground with the other spies; he had seen the same giants and the same walled cities; and God promises that the very land he entered as a scout he will possess as an inheritance. Two things are said of him and they belong together: another spirit and followed me fully. The generation that would not go in had seen God's glory and His miracles in Egypt and in the wilderness and had tempted Him ten times (Numbers 14:22). Forty-five years later Joshua repeats the promise as fact (Joshua 14:9). John uses the same word of a boat: the crowd saw “that one whereinto his disciples were entered” (John 6:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines whereinto as into which, and lists it among the compound relative adverbs of older English.
webster_full: WHEREINTO, adv. Into which.
The doors whereinto they entered.
WHEREIN, adv. In which; as the house wherein he lives.
2. In what; in which thing, time, respect or the like.
WHEREUNTO, adv. To what; to which; used relatively or interrogatively.
scriptures: Numbers 14:24
But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it.
Numbers 14:22
Because all those men which have seen my glory, and my miracles, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice;
Joshua 14:9
And Moses sware on that day, saying, Surely the land whereon thy feet have trodden shall be thine inheritance, and thy children's for ever, because thou hast wholly followed the LORD my God.
John 6:22

The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but that his disciples were gone away alone;
corruption_summary: Caleb's another spirit is read as natural optimism, when Scripture presents it as something God gave and God names.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual application of Numbers 14 makes Caleb the positive thinker and the ten spies the pessimists, so that the lesson becomes a matter of attitude. The text is careful to say something else. God says Caleb had another spirit with him and had followed me fully — the first a possession, the second a course of action, and both spoken by God as His own assessment. Caleb had not seen a smaller enemy; his own speech grants the giants and the cities and answers them with if the LORD delight in us. Faith in Scripture is never the underestimation of a difficulty; it is the accurate weighing of a difficulty against a promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the specificity of the reward. God does not say He will bring Caleb into a land but into the land whereinto he went — the ground he had walked on the reconnaissance, which he later asked for by name: give me this mountain, Hebron, where the Anakim were. Forty-five years of wandering he had not caused stood between the promise and the possession, and he asked for the hardest portion at eighty-five. The generation that refused died in the wilderness, and their children inherited what their fathers would not take.
roots_summary: Hebrew asher ba shammah, “which he went thither” — Numbers 14:24; ruach acheret, another spirit; male achar, to follow fully; Greek eis ho, into which — John 6:22.
roots_lines: Hebrew ruach acheret — another spirit; Numbers 14:24, God's own account of Caleb.
Hebrew male achar — to fill up after, to follow fully; the phrase repeated of Caleb six times.
Hebrew nachalah — an inheritance; Joshua 14:9, the promise made fact.
Greek eis ho — into which; the construction John 6:22 uses of the boat.
English where- compounds — wherein, whereof, whereby, whereunto — ordinary written English in 1611.
usage: “The land whereinto he went” — the very ground he scouted, given as inheritance.
“Because he had another spirit with him” — God's assessment, not a temperament.
“Have tempted me now these ten times” — what the other generation had seen and done.

pos: adv. (to this; the word on which Peter hangs the Christian's calling to suffer patiently, following Christ's steps)
etymology: A compound of here and unto, on the pattern of hereof, hereby, herein — a demonstrative adverb meaning to this. The Greek at 1 Peter 2:21 is eis touto, unto this, standing emphatically at the head of the clause.
biblical_def: The great occurrence is Peter's, and the archaic word carries a doctrine most Christians would rather not read: “For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). The context is servants under harsh masters, taking it patiently when they do well and suffer for it, and Peter says this is your calling. The Greek eis touto is emphatic — unto this you were called. Then he gives the pattern in three strokes: “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22); “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). The last clause is the mechanism. Christ's silence was not indifference to justice; it was the committing of the case to a Judge who will render it. The Preacher uses the word in a very different mood: “For who can eat, or who else can hasten hereunto, more than I?” (Ecclesiastes 2:25) — a man who had every enjoyment asking who was better placed than he to test whether enjoyment satisfies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hereunto as to this, and lists it with the demonstrative compounds hereof, hereby, herein, and hereto.
webster_full: HEREUNTO, adv. To this.
HERETO, adv. To this.
HEREOF, adv. Of this; from this.
HEREBY, adv. By this; by means of this.
HEREIN, adv. In this. Herein is my Father glorified. John 15.
scriptures: 1 Peter 2:21
For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:
1 Peter 2:22
Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:
1 Peter 2:23
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
Ecclesiastes 2:25
For who can eat, or who else can hasten hereunto, more than I?
corruption_summary: Christian calling is preached as fulfilment, gifting, and flourishing, and 1 Peter 2:21 says believers are called to unjust suffering borne patiently.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary teaching on calling concerns vocation, gifting, and the discovery of a life that fits. Peter uses the word for something else entirely: hereunto were ye called — to suffer wrongfully and take it patiently, after the pattern of Christ. It is worth noticing whom he is addressing: household servants, some of them under masters he calls froward, people with no power and no legal recourse. To them the apostle does not say that God will improve their circumstances. He says their situation is where the imitation of Christ actually happens, and that this is what they were called to.

The doctrine must be handled with care, because it has been abused. Peter is not commending passivity toward injustice as such — the same apostle told the Sanhedrin that we ought to obey God rather than men, and the same epistle commands honour to all and a good conscience. Nor is he telling anyone to stay in danger. What he forbids is retaliation and the taking of one's own case in hand, and the alternative he offers is not resignation but committal: Christ committed himself to him that judgeth righteously. That is a transfer of the case to a court that will actually sit, and it is the only ground on which a wronged man can decline to avenge himself without pretending he was not wronged.
roots_summary: Greek eis touto, unto this — 1 Peter 2:21; hupogrammos, a writing-copy for a child to trace — the word rendered example; paradidomi, to commit or hand over — 1 Peter 2:23.
roots_lines: Greek eis touto — unto this; emphatic at the head of 1 Peter 2:21.
Greek hupogrammos — a copyhead written for a child to trace over; rendered example.
Greek ichnos — a footprint, a track; “follow his steps.”
Greek paradidomi — to hand over, commit; 1 Peter 2:23, of Christ committing His case.
Greek loidoreo — to revile; the verb He did not return.
usage: “For even hereunto were ye called” — to suffering borne patiently, said to servants.
Hupogrammos: the copyhead a child traces — the word Peter uses for example.
“Committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” — not resignation, but a transfer of the case.

pos: adv. (of this; twice in the Authorized Version — of the fame of a miracle spreading, and of the reason a high priest must offer for himself)
etymology: A compound of here and of, on the same pattern as hereunto and hereby — a demonstrative adverb meaning of this or from this. The Greek at Hebrews 5:3 is dia tauten, on account of this.
biblical_def: The two occurrences are far apart in tone. Matthew closes the raising of Jairus's daughter with a single sentence: “And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land” (Matthew 9:26). Our Lord had put out the scorners, taken the girl by the hand, and charged that no man should know it — and the report went out anyway, as it always did. The other is doctrinal and carries real weight: “And by reason hereof he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins” (Hebrews 5:3). The hereof points back to the previous verse: the high priest “can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way; for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity” (Hebrews 5:2). His own weakness qualified him to be gentle and obliged him to bring a sacrifice for himself before he could bring one for the people. That double fact is exactly what the writer will use to display the superiority of Christ: “Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hereof as of this, or from this — one of the demonstrative compounds of older English.
webster_full: HEREOF, adv. Of this; from this.
Hereof comes it that prince Harry is valiant.
HEREBY, adv. By this; by means of this.
HEREAT, adv. At this. He was offended hereat.
HEREWITH, adv. With this.
scriptures: Hebrews 5:3
And by reason hereof he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins.
Hebrews 5:2
Who can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way; for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity.
Hebrews 7:27
Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
Matthew 9:26
And the fame hereof went abroad into all that land.
corruption_summary: The priest's own sacrifice is treated as an incidental detail of ritual, when Hebrews makes it the hinge of the whole argument for a better priesthood.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 5:2-3 is often read as background colour before the argument begins, and it is the argument. Every Aaronic high priest had to offer for his own sins first — on the day of atonement, a bullock for himself and his house before the goat for the people — and that requirement is the crack running through the whole system. A mediator who needs a mediator cannot finally mediate. The writer builds the entire case for Christ's superior priesthood on that observation, and lands it in 7:27: He needed no sacrifice for Himself, and the one He offered was Himself, once.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double truth about the old priesthood, because both halves are carried over into the new. Hebrews 5:2 says the priest's own infirmity made him able to have compassion on the ignorant and those out of the way — a sympathy his weakness bought. The writer does not discard that when he moves to Christ; he intensifies it, saying we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. The compassion is kept and the sin removed, which no Levitical priest could offer.
roots_summary: Greek dia tauten, on account of this — Hebrews 5:3; metriopatheo, to bear gently with — Hebrews 5:2; astheneia, infirmity; ephapax, once for all — Hebrews 7:27.
roots_lines: Greek dia tauten — by reason of this; Hebrews 5:3, pointing back to the priest's infirmity.
Greek metriopatheo — to deal gently, moderate one's feeling toward; Hebrews 5:2.
Greek astheneia — weakness, infirmity; what compassed the Aaronic priest about.
Greek ephapax — once for all; Hebrews 7:27, of the single offering of Christ.
Greek pheme — a report or fame; Matthew 9:26, of the news that went abroad.
usage: “By reason hereof he ought… also for himself, to offer for sins” — the crack in the old priesthood.
“He himself also is compassed with infirmity” — the weakness that bought his compassion.
“For this he did once, when he offered up himself” — the answer Hebrews builds toward.

pos: adv. (with this; twice — of Judah unsatisfied with her idolatries, and of the single invitation in Scripture to put God to the test)
etymology: A compound of here and with, on the pattern of hereof and hereunto. The Hebrew at Malachi 3:10 is ba-zoth, in or by this — the demonstrative pointing at the specific act commanded in the same verse.
biblical_def: Two occurrences, and they are opposites. Ezekiel of Judah's appetite for idols: “Thou hast moreover multiplied thy fornication in the land of Canaan unto Chaldea; and yet thou wast not satisfied herewith” (Ezekiel 16:29) — the settled character of idolatry is that it does not satisfy and therefore always requires more. Malachi contains the other, and it is one of the most remarkable sentences God speaks: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it” (Malachi 3:10). Everywhere else Scripture forbids tempting God — our Lord answers Satan with it — and here God invites a test, in one narrow matter, having first laid a charge: “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings” (Malachi 3:8). The promise attached is not money but protection: “I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes” (Malachi 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines herewith as with this — one of the demonstrative compounds standing beside hereof, hereat, and hereunto.
webster_full: HEREWITH, adv. With this.
HEREOF, adv. Of this; from this.
HEREAT, adv. At this.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of any thing; but appropriately, the tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock.
STOREHOUSE, n. A house or building for keeping grain or goods of any kind; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
scriptures: Malachi 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
Malachi 3:8
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
Malachi 3:11
And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts.
Ezekiel 16:29
Thou hast moreover multiplied thy fornication in the land of Canaan unto Chaldea; and yet thou wast not satisfied herewith.
corruption_summary: Malachi 3:10 has been made a promise of financial return on giving, when the invitation is narrow, the charge is theft, and the promise is protection.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse is more heavily used in fundraising, and the use consistently omits three things. First the charge that occasions it: the people are accused of robbing God, and the tithe is not presented as an investment opportunity but as a debt already owed and withheld. Second the object: the tithe goes into the storehouse that there may be meat in mine house — the support of the ministering Levites, not a general principle of return. Third the promise itself: the windows of heaven and the rebuke of the devourer concern rain and crops in an agrarian covenant nation whose harvests were tied by covenant to obedience, and the following verse says so plainly.

There is a further caution about the invitation. Prove me now herewith is unique — God elsewhere forbids the testing of Himself, and our Lord answered the tempter with Deuteronomy 6:16. To generalise Malachi 3:10 into a licence for believers to set God tests of their own devising inverts it; the test is God's, in a matter God specified, addressed to men already convicted of a specific theft. What the passage does establish, and what should not be surrendered along with the abuses, is that God takes seriously how His people handle what is His, that withholding it is called robbery, and that He is not in anyone's debt when they stop.

Hebrew bachan — to test, prove, assay metal; the verb of the invitation.
Hebrew okel — the devourer, the eater; Malachi 3:11, rebuked for their sakes.
usage: “Prove me now herewith” — the one invitation to test God, in one specified matter.
“Will a man rob God?” — the charge that occasions the invitation.
“Yet thou wast not satisfied herewith” — the settled character of idolatry.

pos: adv. (from that; the word of the charge not to turn aside from the law, and of the kings who did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam)
etymology: A compound of there and from, on the pattern of thereof, therein, thereat, thereto — a demonstrative adverb meaning from that. The Hebrew idiom is sur min, to turn aside from, or lo sar min, he departed not from.
biblical_def: The same word marks the best and the worst of Israel's history, and the contrast is deliberate. Joshua's farewell charge: “Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, that ye turn not aside therefrom to the right hand or to the left” (Joshua 23:6), repeating Moses in Deuteronomy 5:32. Two things are worth noting: courage is required to keep a law, not merely to fight a battle; and the departure may be in either direction, adding to the law being as much a turning aside as subtracting. Then the identical construction becomes the historian's standing verdict on the kings of Israel. Of Jehoram: “Nevertheless he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom” (2 Kings 3:3). Of Jehoahaz: “he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom” (2 Kings 13:2). The formula recurs through the northern kingdom until the exile: a whole dynasty of men who did not depart from a sin instituted two centuries earlier for reasons of state.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines therefrom as from this or from that, and lists it among the demonstrative compounds thereof, therein, thereat, and thereto.
webster_full: THEREFROM, adv. From this or from that.
Turn not aside therefrom, to the right hand or to the left. Josh. 23.
THEREOF, adv. Of that or this.
THEREIN, adv. In that or this place, time or thing.
THERETO, adv. To that or this.
scriptures: Joshua 23:6
Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, that ye turn not aside therefrom to the right hand or to the left;
Deuteronomy 5:32
Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.
2 Kings 3:3
Nevertheless he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom.
2 Kings 13:2
And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom.
corruption_summary: Departures from Scripture are imagined as running in one direction only, so a church guards one flank and loses the other.
corruption_paragraphs: To the right hand or to the left is a formula, and it is exact. Turning aside from God's word is possible in two directions, and every generation of the church watches one of them intently while walking off the other. The party alarmed by liberalism polices subtraction — the doctrines quietly dropped — and adds requirements Scripture never made, binding consciences on matters God left free. The party alarmed by legalism polices addition and quietly lets the hard commands go. Joshua's charge covers both by naming the road rather than the ditch: keep and do all that is written, and turn aside neither way.

The Jeroboam formula shows how a departure becomes permanent. Jeroboam set up calves at Bethel and Dan for a stated political reason — lest the people go up to Jerusalem to sacrifice and their hearts turn again to the house of David — and every northern king after him inherited the arrangement and kept it. The historian's refrain is not that they invented new wickedness but that they departed not therefrom. Institutional sin is rarely re-decided; it is simply not departed from, and the men who maintain it usually have no strong feelings about it at all. It required courage to keep the law, exactly as Joshua said, and no courage whatever to leave the calves standing.
roots_summary: Hebrew sur min, to turn aside from — Joshua 23:6; lo sar min, he departed not from — 2 Kings 3:3, 13:2; dabaq, to cleave — 2 Kings 3:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew sur — to turn aside, depart; the verb in both the charge and the verdict.
Hebrew yamin u-semol — right hand and left; the two directions of departure.
Hebrew dabaq — to cling, cleave; 2 Kings 3:3, of Jehoram cleaving to Jeroboam's sins.
Hebrew chazaq — to be strong, courageous; Joshua 23:6, required for keeping the law.
English there- compounds — thereof, therein, thereat, therefrom — ordinary in 1611.
usage: “Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written” — courage, for a law.
“To the right hand or to the left” — departure runs in two directions.
“He departed not therefrom” — the refrain over a whole dynasty.

pos: adv. (at that place or thing; of the laver where priests washed before service, and of the wide gate that many go in at)
etymology: A compound of there and at, meaning at that. The Hebrew at Exodus 30:19 is mimmennu, from it; the Greek at Matthew 7:13 is di autes, through it — the Authorized Version's thereat standing for the gate itself.
biblical_def: Two of the three occurrences concern the brasen laver: “For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat” (Exodus 30:19), and its execution, “And Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet thereat” (Exodus 40:31). The command is given with a penalty attached — they shall wash, that they die not — and it is worth seeing what it means. These men had already been consecrated and washed once at their ordination; the laver was for the daily defilement of hands that handled sacrifices and feet that walked an unpaved court. The distinction between the washing of regeneration, which is not repeated, and the daily cleansing of a believer's walk is exactly the distinction our Lord makes to Peter: he that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet. The third occurrence is one of the most sobering sentences our Lord spoke: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat” (Matthew 7:13), and against it, “strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Matthew 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thereat as at that place, or at that thing or event — on account of that.
webster_full: THEREAT, adv. At that place.
Wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat. Matt. 7.
2. At that; on account of that.
Every error is a stain to the beauty of nature; for which cause it blusheth thereat.
LAVER, n. A vessel for washing; a large basin. Ex. 30.
scriptures: Matthew 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Matthew 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Exodus 30:19
For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat:
Exodus 40:31
And Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet thereat:
corruption_summary: The two ways are read as two equally respectable options, and the arithmetic our Lord attaches — many and few — is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:13-14 is unpopular for one reason: it counts. Our Lord does not merely say there are two roads; He says which one most people are on. The pluralist assumption of the age is that sincere seekers along many paths arrive at the same place, and that any claim to a narrow way is arrogance. The passage forecloses it, and it does so in the Sermon on the Mount, in the plainest language, from the lips of Christ Himself. He is also the one who said I am the way and no man cometh unto the Father but by me. A gospel that will not say few there be that find it is not preaching what He preached.

The universalist evasion works the same ground from the other side: the narrow gate is granted, and then everyone is eventually said to pass through it. That reading has to ignore leadeth to destruction and everything our Lord says about the last judgment two chapters later, where He tells men He never knew them. The laver texts supply the pastoral counterpart. The gate is entered once; the hands and feet are washed daily, on pain of death, because service in the holy place does not exempt a man from defilement in it. Both truths are needed: the entering is settled, and the washing is not finished.
roots_summary: Hebrew kiyyor, the laver — Exodus 30:19; rachats, to wash; Greek stenos, narrow — Matthew 7:13; eureia, broad; apoleia, destruction.
roots_lines: Hebrew kiyyor — the brasen laver; Exodus 30:18-21, set between the tent and the altar.
Hebrew rachats — to wash; the daily washing of hands and feet, on pain of death.
Greek stenos — narrow, strait; Matthew 7:13-14, of the gate that leads to life.
Greek platus and eurus — broad and wide; of the other way.
Greek apoleia — destruction, perdition; where the broad way leads.
usage: “Many there be which go in thereat” — our Lord counts, and the count is unwelcome.
“Few there be that find it” — the answering half of the sentence.
“Shall wash their hands and their feet thereat” — daily cleansing for consecrated men.

pos: adv. (from this time forward; of the law binding on all generations, and of the sentence our Lord passed on a barren fig tree)
etymology: A compound of hence — Old English heonan, from here — with forward. The Greek at Matthew 21:19 is eis ton aiona, unto the age, an emphatic for ever; the Hebrew at Numbers 15:23 is ve-halah, and onward.
biblical_def: Numbers uses the word for the perpetual reach of the law: the LORD had commanded “by the hand of Moses, from the day that the LORD commanded Moses, and henceforward among your generations” (Numbers 15:23). Whatever else changed, the commandment ran forward through the generations, and the chapter goes on to distinguish sins of ignorance, for which a sacrifice was provided, from the sin of a high hand, for which there was none. The second occurrence is a sentence: “when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away” (Matthew 21:19). It is our Lord's only destructive miracle, performed the morning after He cleansed the temple, on a tree that was carrying leaves — the sign of fruit — and no fruit. The disciples marvelled at how soon it withered, and He answered them about faith: “If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed… it shall be done” (Matthew 21:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines henceforward as from this time forward, and treats it as equivalent to henceforth.
webster_full: HENCEFORWARD, adv. From this time forward; henceforth.
HENCEFORTH, adv. From this time forward.
HENCE, adv. From this place.
2. From this time; in the future; as, a week hence.
3. From this cause or reason, noting a consequence, inference or deduction.
scriptures: Matthew 21:19

And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered away.
Matthew 21:21

Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.
Numbers 15:23
Even all that the LORD hath commanded you by the hand of Moses, from the day that the LORD commanded Moses, and henceforward among your generations;
Matthew 21:13
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
corruption_summary: The cursing of the fig tree is dismissed as a display of temper, when Matthew places it deliberately around the cleansing of the temple.
corruption_paragraphs: Sceptical readers regularly cite this miracle as evidence of a petulant Jesus destroying a tree for not bearing fruit out of season, and some Christian commentators seem embarrassed enough to hurry past it. Matthew's arrangement answers the objection. The cursing sits immediately beside the cleansing of the temple, where our Lord had found the same thing — a great show of religious activity and no fruit — and quoted Jeremiah: ye have made it a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13). A fig tree in leaf advertises fruit, since on the fig the early fruit comes with or before the leaves; a tree with leaves and nothing else is making a claim it cannot honour. That is precisely the charge against the temple, and the acted parable makes it visible.

Numbers 15:23 supplies the other half of the doctrine, and it is a mercy. The law ran forward through the generations, and the same chapter provides a sacrifice for the congregation and for the individual who sinned unwittingly. The permanence of God's commandment is not a trap; it is accompanied by provision, and the only case excluded is the man who acts presumptuously with a high hand, who reproaches the LORD and is cut off. Leaves without fruit and a high hand against the law are the two conditions Scripture treats as beyond the ordinary remedies — and both are conditions of pretence rather than of weakness.
roots_summary: Greek eis ton aiona, unto the age, for ever — Matthew 21:19; xeraino, to dry up, wither; Hebrew ve-halah, and onward — Numbers 15:23.
roots_lines: Greek eis ton aiona — unto the age; the emphatic “for ever” of the sentence on the tree.
Greek xeraino — to dry up, wither; Matthew 21:19, of what happened presently.
Greek parachrema — immediately, on the spot; the word rendered presently.
Hebrew ve-halah — and onward, henceforward; Numbers 15:23.
Hebrew yad ramah — a high hand; Numbers 15:30, the presumptuous sin with no sacrifice.
usage: “Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever” — leaves, and no fruit.
“Henceforward among your generations” — the law running forward, with provision attached.
“Ye have made it a den of thieves” — the same charge, the day before.

pos: adv. and prep. (an older form of among; twice in the Authorized Version, and one of the two is the first hiding-place in human history)
etymology: From Old English on gemang, in a crowd or mingling, with the adverbial -st added in Middle English. The Hebrew at Genesis 3:8 is be-thok, in the midst of. The Authorized Version prefers among almost everywhere; amongst survives only twice.
biblical_def: The word is a variant of among and needs no defining; what needs attention is where the translators left it standing. “And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8). Every element of the fall's aftermath is in that sentence. The voice is the same voice that had spoken the world into being and had walked there before; the trees are the trees He planted; the hiding is a man attempting to put created things between himself and his Creator. It does not work, and God's response is a question He did not need answered: “And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). Adam's reply names the new facts: “I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). Fear of God, shame at the body, and concealment all enter the world in one verse. The psalmist states the futility of the attempt for all time: “Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?” (Psalm 139:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats amongst as a variant of among, meaning mingled or conjoined with, and notes it is used chiefly in the more formal register.
webster_full: AMONGST, prep. Mingled or conjoined with a number of other objects; the same as among.
AMONG, prep. In a general or primitive sense, mixed or mingled with; as tares among wheat.
2. Conjoined or associated with, or making part of the number.
3. Of the number; as, there is not one among a thousand.
MINGLE, v.t. To mix; to blend; to unite in one body.
scriptures: Genesis 3:8
And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.
Genesis 3:9
And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
Genesis 3:10
And he said, I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.
Psalm 139:7
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
corruption_summary: Genesis 3 is filed as myth explaining the human condition, which removes the historical Adam that Paul's doctrine of sin and salvation requires.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic treatment reads Genesis 3 as an etiological tale — a story about why humans feel shame, fear death, and struggle with the soil — and holds that its truth is unaffected by whether it happened. The New Testament will not permit the separation. Paul's argument in Romans 5 turns entirely on one man through whom sin entered and death by sin, set against one man through whom the free gift came; 1 Corinthians 15 sets the first man Adam against the last Adam; 1 Timothy 2 grounds an instruction on the order of the creation and the deception of Eve. A mythic Adam cannot bear a historical imputation, and if the imputation of guilt in the first man is figurative, the imputation of righteousness in the second is not secured.

The verse itself is also more precise than a myth would be. God does not find Adam; God calls him. The question Where art thou? is not an enquiry but a summons, the first act of the seeking God, and it precedes the sentence, the curse on the serpent, and the promise of the seed who shall bruise his head. Before God passes judgment He goes looking, and before He drives them out He clothes them with coats of skins — the first death in Scripture, occurring so that guilty people might be covered. The trees were a poor hiding place and God provided a better covering than leaves.
roots_summary: Hebrew be-thok, in the midst of — Genesis 3:8; chaba, to hide oneself; qol, voice or sound; ayyekkah, where art thou — Genesis 3:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew be-thok — in the midst of, among; Genesis 3:8, of the trees of the garden.
Hebrew chaba — to withdraw and hide oneself; the verb of Adam and his wife.
Hebrew qol — a voice or sound; what they heard walking in the garden.
Hebrew ayyekkah — where art thou; Genesis 3:9, the first question God asks fallen man.
Old English on gemang — in a mingling; the source of among and amongst.
usage: “Hid themselves… amongst the trees of the garden” — created things put between man and God.
“Where art thou?” — a summons, not an enquiry.
“Whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — the futility stated for all time.

pos: adv. (on foot; of the multitude who outran a boat to reach Christ, and of Paul's deliberate choice to walk from Troas to Assos alone)
etymology: From a-, the old reduced preposition on, and foot — the same formation as abed, ashore, asleep. The Greek at Mark 6:33 is peze, on foot or by land; the same adverb at Acts 20:13.
biblical_def: Both occurrences describe a journey chosen over an easier one. Mark: when Jesus and the disciples withdrew by boat to a desert place, “the people saw them departing, and many knew him, and ran afoot thither out of all cities, and outwent them, and came together unto him” (Mark 6:33). They ran around the head of the lake, from several towns, and arrived first — the crowd beat the boat. Our Lord had gone to that place for rest, having just heard of the death of John the Baptist and having received the apostles back from their mission; He found five thousand men waiting. The verse that follows is the measure of Him: “Jesus, when he came out, saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd: and he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34). The second is Paul at Troas: “we went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot” (Acts 20:13). Luke records the arrangement without explanation. Paul sent his companions round by sea and walked some twenty miles over the headland alone, on his way to Jerusalem and bonds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines afoot as on foot, borne by the feet, walking — and figuratively as in action or in a state of being planned.
webster_full: AFOOT, adv. On foot; borne by the feet; opposed to riding.
2. In action; in a state of being planned for execution.
A design is afoot.
AFOOT, in a military sense, on foot; as infantry.
FOOT, n. The lower extremity of the leg of an animal, on which it stands and walks.
scriptures: Mark 6:33
And the people saw them departing, and many knew him, and ran afoot thither out of all cities, and outwent them, and came together unto him.
Mark 6:34
And Jesus, when he came out, saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd: and he began to teach them many things.
Acts 20:13
And we went before to ship, and sailed unto Assos, there intending to take in Paul: for so had he appointed, minding himself to go afoot.
Mark 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
corruption_summary: Christ's compassion is presented as unlimited availability, and the same chapter shows Him deliberately withdrawing for rest — both are in the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 6 is used in two opposite and equally partial ways. One holds up verse 34 — moved with compassion, and He began to teach them many things — as the model of a ministry always available, and uses it to press pastors and Christian workers past every limit. The other holds up verse 31 — Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while — as a warrant for guarding one's own time. Both verses are in the same chapter, spoken by the same Lord, about the same afternoon. He deliberately sought rest for His disciples and for Himself, and when the rest was interrupted by need He met the need and then, after feeding them, sent the multitude away and went up into a mountain to pray.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that neither withdrawal nor availability is a rule; the Lord did both and there is no formula in the chapter. What is not optional is the compassion, and Mark gives its ground: they were as sheep not having a shepherd, a phrase drawn from Numbers 27 and Ezekiel 34, where God indicts the shepherds of Israel and promises to come Himself. Paul's twenty miles over the headland belongs to the same register. Luke records no reason, and men have guessed at prayer, at grief, at the need to be alone before Jerusalem; the fact recorded is simply that he sent the ship round and walked.
roots_summary: Greek peze, on foot, by land — Mark 6:33, Acts 20:13; splagchnizomai, to be moved in the bowels with compassion — Mark 6:34; poimen, a shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek peze — on foot, by land; Mark 6:33 and Acts 20:13, the only two occurrences.
Greek splagchnizomai — to be moved in the inward parts; the strongest word for compassion.
Greek poimen — a shepherd; Mark 6:34, drawing on Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34.
Greek proerchomai — to go before, outrun; the crowd outwent the boat.
Old English on fot — on foot; the source of the English adverb.
usage: “Ran afoot thither out of all cities, and outwent them” — the crowd beat the boat.
“As sheep not having a shepherd” — the ground of His compassion.
“Minding himself to go afoot” — Paul walked, and Luke gives no reason.
